nodes.name: Conversation Turn Lifecycle
nodes.description:
A person sends one message in a chat app and expects one useful answer back. Answering can detour through a sign-in, a confirmation the user has to tap, or a conversation so long the assistant can no longer hold all of it. This subsystem owns that single round trip, from an arriving message to a sent reply and an up-to-date conversation memory.

The terms this subsystem uses, and what each means here:

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| Turn | One incoming message and the single reply that answers it. |
| Conversation | The scope memory and waiting confirmations belong to: one user on one platform, narrowed to one thread where the platform has threads. |
| History | The remembered earlier exchanges handed to the assistant so it can follow along. |
| Pending approval | A sensitive action held back until the user confirms it. |
| Reply | The one answer a turn produces: a short line, a card, or a set of option cards. |

Outside this boundary: how each chat platform receives a message and paints a reply in its own style, how the assistant's tools are connected and authorized, and where long-lived sign-ins are kept. Those neighbours hand a turn in and render what it produces; they never decide what a turn does.

nodes.name: Turn
nodes.description:
One exchange: an arriving user message and the single reply that answers it. Everything a turn needs is gathered at the start (who is speaking, what was said before, whether a confirmation is waiting) and everything it changes is committed at the end, so an interrupted turn leaves nothing half-written.

Rules that always hold:

- A turn ends with exactly one reply: a short line, one card, or one set of option cards, never a mix.
- A turn that pauses for a confirmation records nothing; the work in flight travels with the held confirmation instead.
- Memory that cannot be read is discarded rather than allowed to wedge the conversation.

Lifecycle:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Running: message arrives
    Running --> Paused: sensitive action needs confirmation
    Paused --> Running: user answers
    Running --> Answered: reply sent, memory updated
    Answered --> [*]
```

A turn reaches the conversation's memory and any waiting confirmation through the conversation it belongs to, never by holding either itself.

nodes.name: Conversation History
nodes.description:
What the assistant remembers of a conversation, so it can follow along instead of starting cold on every message. Memory is kept per conversation: one user on one platform, narrowed to a single thread where the platform has threads, so two parallel threads with the same person never bleed into each other.

Rules that always hold:

- Each recorded exchange ages out on its own; nothing is kept forever.
- Only a bounded number of the most recent exchanges is kept.
- Memory that can no longer be read is dropped rather than allowed to block the conversation.

Lifecycle: starts empty, grows by one entry per answered turn, is summarized when it approaches what the assistant can read at once, and is cleared outright when something makes the earlier exchanges untrue, such as the user signing out.

nodes.name: Pending Approval
nodes.description:
A sensitive action held back until the user says yes. When the assistant wants to use something the tool provider marked destructive, the action does not run: the work already in flight is set aside and the user is shown a confirmation with Confirm and Cancel.

Rules that always hold:

- At most one confirmation waits per conversation, and picking it up consumes it, so the same held work can never run twice.
- The confirmation ages out on its own, and held work that can no longer be read counts as expired.
- One answer decides every action held in that pause.

Lifecycle: held, then either answered (confirmed, cancelled, or abandoned when the user changes topic) or quietly expired, after which the user's next message is treated as a fresh question.

nodes.name: Chat User
nodes.description:
The person talking to the assistant in a chat app, today Slack, LINE, or Discord. Every turn runs on their behalf, and any sign-in to a connected service is held against their identity rather than shared.

They are identified by a stable handle combining the platform, the workspace or account, and the user, so the same person in two workspaces counts as two users and shares neither memory nor sign-in. A person, never a system: automated callers do not enter through this subsystem.

nodes.name: Run Turn
nodes.description:
Answer one incoming message. This is the single entry point for the whole round trip: gather what was said before, pick up any confirmation the user might be answering, show that work is under way, ask the assistant for an answer, send it, and bring the conversation memory up to date.

- **Issued by**: the chat user, relayed by whichever platform received the message.
- **Requires**: message text, plus a resolved identity and conversation scope.
- **Produces**: exactly one reply, and then either an updated memory or a held confirmation.
- **Fails as**: an authorization the user was offered but never finished is an expected ending and passes quietly; anything else is a real failure, logged, and the user's message goes unanswered.

nodes.name: Compact History
nodes.description:
Summarize the older part of a conversation once the previous exchange came close to what the assistant can read at one time, so a long conversation keeps working instead of hitting the ceiling.

The most recent exchange is kept word for word and everything before it collapses into a single summary that preserves names, identifiers, links, dates, numbers, and anything still unresolved. Small talk, retries, and corrected mistakes are dropped.

Runs at the start of a turn, before the assistant reads the conversation. Memory that cannot be read is left untouched rather than summarized, and a conversation still well under the limit is left alone.

nodes.name: Commit Turn History
nodes.description:
Record what this turn said and heard, so the next message picks up where this one left off. Runs once the reply has reached the user, adding this turn's messages as one entry with its own expiry.

Not every turn records something:

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| An ordinary turn | This turn's messages are added as a single entry. |
| The turn paused for a confirmation | Nothing is recorded; the messages travel with the held confirmation and are recorded once the user answers. |
| The turn made the earlier exchanges untrue, for example the user signed out | Nothing is added; the conversation is forgotten instead. |

Adding an entry also ages out the oldest one once the conversation is already remembering as much as it keeps.

nodes.name: Load History
nodes.description:
Read back the remembered exchanges of a conversation so the assistant can follow along. Called at the very start of every turn, before anything else happens.

The answer is current as of the read: exchanges that have aged out are simply absent, and their leftover placeholders are tidied on the next write. The turn itself and the summarizer are the only callers.

nodes.name: Park Approval
nodes.description:
Hold a sensitive action back and ask the user to confirm it before it runs. Raised when the assistant tries to use a tool its provider marked destructive.

The work already in flight is set aside together with the held action, and the user is shown a confirmation naming what is about to happen, with Confirm and Cancel offered as tappable replies. The turn ends here having recorded nothing, because the exchange is not finished: it completes when the user answers.

Only one confirmation waits per conversation, and it expires on its own if the user never comes back to it.

nodes.name: Answer Approval
nodes.description:
The user's response to a waiting confirmation, which arrives as their next message, whether they tap one of the offered buttons or type something else.

- **Confirm**: the held action runs and the turn finishes as if it had never paused.
- **Cancel**: the action is dropped and the assistant acknowledges briefly, without implying that anything went wrong or that permission was refused.
- **Anything else**: the user has moved on, so the held action is dropped silently and their new message is answered instead.

The confirmation is consumed the moment it is picked up, so it can never be answered twice, and one answer settles every action held in that pause. The wording the user must match is the wording the confirmation itself offered, so a reply still works when the user's language cannot be resolved a second time.

nodes.name: Reply Sent
nodes.description:
The user has received the turn's answer: a short line, one card, or a set of option cards.

Fires after the assistant has settled on an answer and the platform has rendered it. It marks the point where the turn's promise to the user is kept, and it is what puts the conversation memory in motion: an ordinary turn is recorded from here, while a turn that made the earlier exchanges untrue forgets the conversation instead. A turn that paused for a confirmation never reaches this point at all.

nodes.name: History Compacted
nodes.description:
The older part of a conversation has been replaced by a summary.

Fires at the start of a turn, before the assistant reads the conversation, and only when the previous exchange came close to the reading limit. From here on the assistant works from the summary plus the latest exchange, and the replaced entries are gone for good. Stays inside this subsystem.

nodes.name: Approval Requested
nodes.description:
A sensitive action has been held back and the user has been shown a confirmation naming it.

The turn is paused rather than finished, and nothing has been recorded. What happens next belongs to the user: confirm, cancel, or move on and let the request quietly expire. The confirmation the user sees is what carries the wording their answer will be matched against.

nodes.name: Approval Answered
nodes.description:
The user has responded to a waiting confirmation, by confirming it, cancelling it, or moving on to something else.

The held work resumes with that one decision applied to every action in the pause, and the exchange that began when the confirmation was raised finally completes and is recorded as a single entry.

nodes.name: One Reply Per Turn
nodes.description:
Every turn ends with exactly one reply: a short line, a single card, or a single set of option cards, never a mix and never several messages in a row.

The business cares because the user is sitting in a chat window. Two half-answers, or an answer with loose text beside it, read as a malfunction and make it unclear which part to act on. One shape also lets every chat platform render the same answer natively, so a reply looks at home everywhere without the assistant knowing where it landed.

The assistant is told this up front, the answer it produces can only take one of the three shapes, and the turn dispatches exactly one of them. Applies to every turn, including a resumed one.

nodes.name: Paused Turn Records Nothing
nodes.description:
A turn that pauses for a confirmation must not write anything to the conversation memory. The messages in flight travel with the held confirmation and come back when the user answers.

The business cares because recording them here would either wipe the conversation outright or separate a held action from the result it produces later, leaving the assistant referring to work the user cannot see and cannot finish. Nothing surfaces to the user directly; the symptom would be an assistant that has lost the thread on the very next message.

Applies whenever an action is held, and only then.

nodes.name: One Decision Covers Every Held Action
nodes.description:
When a single pause holds more than one action, the user's one Confirm or Cancel decides all of them.

The business cares because the user is shown one confirmation and answers it once. Anything left undecided would strand the turn with no way to finish and no second question to answer, so the user would be stuck waiting on something they already responded to. Violation would surface as a turn that never replies.

Applies to every pause that holds more than one action.

nodes.name: Unreadable Memory Never Blocks a Conversation
nodes.description:
When remembered exchanges or held work can no longer be read, they are discarded and the user's message is answered as a fresh start.

The business cares because the alternative is a conversation that is permanently stuck: every message fails the same way, and the damaged memory is exactly the thing the user has no way to reach or clear. Losing earlier context is recoverable in one message; a wedged conversation is not recoverable at all. The user sees an assistant that has forgotten the earlier discussion, never an error.

Applies alike to the conversation memory, to summarizing it, and to a held confirmation whose set-aside work no longer decodes.

nodes.name: Forget Conversation
nodes.description:
Drop everything remembered about a conversation, so the user's next message is answered as if it were their first.

- **Issued by**: the turn itself, not the user directly, once something that happened during the turn made the earlier exchanges untrue. Today the one thing that does this is the user signing out of the connected services.
- **Requires**: nothing. It is safe on a conversation that remembers nothing.
- **Produces**: an empty memory. Every recorded exchange and any summary standing in for older ones are gone for good.
- **Fails as**: it does not. Forgetting is best-effort and repeating it changes nothing.

Runs instead of recording the turn, never alongside it: the turn that triggered the forgetting is itself discarded along with everything before it, because its answer also assumed what is no longer true.

nodes.name: Earlier Exchanges Invalidated
nodes.description:
Something this turn did has made the remembered exchanges untrue, so they can no longer be relied on.

Today the only thing that raises it is the user signing out of every connected service: the earlier answers were built on an authorization that no longer exists, so quoting them back would describe access the user has just taken away.

Fires after the reply has reached the user and in place of the moment the memory would ordinarily be brought up to date. The conversation is forgotten in response. Stays inside this subsystem.

nodes.name: Conversation Forgotten
nodes.description: Everything remembered about a conversation is gone, including any summary standing in for older exchanges. The user's next message is answered cold.

nodes.name: Turn History Committed
nodes.description:
The conversation memory now includes this turn, as a single entry carrying its own expiry.

Fires last in an ordinary turn, after the reply has reached the user. From here the next message has something to pick up from. Nothing reacts to it.

nodes.name: Remembered Exchanges Age Out
nodes.description:
Every recorded exchange carries its own expiry, a week by default, and disappears on its own once it passes. Nothing is remembered indefinitely.

The business cares because an assistant that quotes a months-old exchange back at someone is both unhelpful and a liability: the user stopped expecting it to remember long ago, and the content is often something they would rather was not still sitting around. Ageing each exchange separately, rather than the conversation as a whole, means an active discussion keeps its recent context while the stale tail falls away underneath it.

Nothing surfaces to the user. An aged-out exchange is simply absent when the memory is read, and the pointer it left behind is tidied on the next write. Applies to every exchange in every conversation.

nodes.name: Only the Most Recent Exchanges Are Kept
nodes.description:
A conversation remembers at most a fixed number of its most recent exchanges, ten by default. Recording one more drops the oldest.

The business cares because everything remembered is re-read on every single message: the cost of a turn and the wait before the user sees an answer both grow with the length of the memory, and there is a hard ceiling on how much the assistant can read at all. Capping the count keeps an ordinary conversation cheap and quick, and leaves summarizing to handle the harder case where even a handful of exchanges have grown too long. A summary counts as one of the kept exchanges.

Nothing surfaces to the user; they see an assistant that follows the recent thread but has lost the very beginning of a long discussion. Applies to every conversation.

nodes.name: Memory Is Scoped to One Conversation
nodes.description:
What is remembered belongs to one user on one platform, narrowed further to a single thread where the platform has threads. No conversation can read another's memory.

The business cares because the same person often runs two unrelated discussions side by side, and letting one bleed into the other produces answers that look like the assistant has confused two people, or that pull something from a private thread into a shared one. Where the platform has no threads, the whole dialog with that person is one conversation, which is the behaviour the user expects there.

Nothing surfaces as an error; a violation shows up as an answer referring to something the user never said in this conversation. Applies to every read and every write of the memory.

nodes.name: Summarize Only Near the Reading Limit
nodes.description:
Summarizing runs only once the previous exchange genuinely came close to what the assistant can read at one time, at four fifths of that limit, and then aims to shrink the older part to roughly a fifth of its length. A conversation still comfortably under the limit is left exactly as it is.

The business cares because summarizing is not free in either direction. Doing it early spends an extra model run on every long-ish conversation and permanently throws away detail that was never in the way. Doing it late, or not at all, means a conversation that simply stops working once it outgrows the limit, with no warning to the user and nothing they can do about it.

The measurement is what the assistant actually read on its last real answer rather than an estimate, so the trigger tracks reality including bulky tool output. When the assistant's reading limit cannot be determined, a deliberately low one is assumed, so summarizing fires early rather than never. Applies to this operation only.

nodes.name: The Latest Exchange Is Never Summarized
nodes.description:
The most recent complete exchange is kept word for word; only what came before it collapses into a summary. Where the split falls is constrained too: it must land on a plain message from the user, never partway through an exchange still waiting on results from a tool.

The business cares on two counts. The latest exchange is the thing the user is actually talking about right now, so paraphrasing it makes the assistant's very next answer wrong about the question in front of it. And splitting through a half-finished exchange separates work already in flight from the request that started it, which the assistant then refuses to read at all: the conversation stops working outright rather than merely getting vaguer.

When no safe split point exists, nothing is summarized and the conversation is left untouched. Applies to this operation only.

nodes.name: A Summary Keeps the Hard Facts
nodes.description:
A summary must carry over who the user is, what they asked for, what the assistant did or found out, and anything still unfinished, with names, reference numbers, email addresses, links, dates, and figures reproduced exactly as they appeared. Small talk, retries, and mistakes already corrected are dropped. It reads as plain prose in the conversation's own language.

The business cares because the summary is the only thing left of the earlier discussion. A reference number that gets rounded off or an address that gets paraphrased is a fact the user has to supply all over again, and an unfinished request that quietly vanishes is a promise the assistant made and then broke without ever saying so. Chatter, by contrast, costs nothing to lose, which makes the trade entirely one-sided.

Nothing surfaces as an error; the symptom is an assistant that asks for something the user already gave it, or that has forgotten it still owes them an answer. Applies to this operation only.

nodes.name: Assistant Run and Tool Access
nodes.description:
An assistant that can only talk is not much use. Being useful means reaching outside itself into services the user already has accounts with, acting there on that user's own permission rather than a shared one, and stopping short of anything irreversible until the user has said yes. This subsystem owns exactly that: what the assistant can reach, whose permission it reaches with, and which of those actions have to be confirmed first.

The terms this subsystem uses, and what each means here:

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| Tool provider | An outside service that offers its capabilities to the assistant, either a standing MCP server or an API description this product serves as one. |
| Tool | One thing a provider can do, which the assistant may call while working out an answer. |
| Sign-in | One person's own grant of access to one connected service, given once inside the conversation and reused afterwards. |
| Sensitive tool | A tool its provider marks as destructive, which never runs before the user confirms it. |
| Assistant run | One pass of the assistant over the user's message, the remembered exchanges, and the tools it can currently reach. |

Outside this boundary: the round trip around a run, meaning reading the conversation memory, sending the reply, and recording it, along with the confirmation card the user actually answers, all of which belong to the conversation neighbour; how each chat platform paints the sign-in link; and the credentials the product's own chat apps need to post at all.

nodes.name: Assistant Run
nodes.description:
One pass of the assistant over what the user just said, what was said before, and the tools it can reach right now. The pass is assembled fresh every time: the product's own standing guidance, the chat platform's formatting dialect, the language to answer in, and a live connection to every configured tool provider.

Rules that always hold:

- The tools it holds are the only capabilities it may claim; it never offers something no tool can do.
- Anything arriving from a tool result or an earlier exchange is treated as information, never as an instruction to follow.
- The answer follows the language of the user's own message, falling back to their platform language only when the message leaves it unclear.

Lifecycle:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Prepared: guidance and tools assembled
    Prepared --> Working: calls tools, up to three attempts at a malformed answer
    Working --> Answered: settles on one answer
    Working --> Held: a sensitive tool needs the user's yes
    Answered --> [*]
    Held --> [*]
```

A run either answers or stops holding one or more sensitive actions. It never sends the answer itself and never records anything; the conversation round trip around it does both.

nodes.name: Tool Provider Connection
nodes.description:
The live link between one assistant run and one tool provider. It is opened fresh for each run and closed with it, and it carries the identity of the person the run is for, so everything the provider does happens on their account rather than a shared one.

Rules that always hold:

- Every tool the provider marks as destructive is held for the user's confirmation before it runs.
- A provider that expects a sign-in is reached with that person's stored one, and starts a new sign-in when there is none.
- A provider that expects no sign-in is reached as an anonymous caller, with nothing stored for it.

Lifecycle: opened for the run, possibly pausing part-way while the user signs in, then serving tool calls until the run finishes. Nothing about the connection survives the run except the sign-in it may have obtained.

nodes.name: Service Authorization
nodes.description:
What one person has granted the assistant on one connected service, so a sign-in they completed once keeps working on every later request. It is held against that person and that service together: two colleagues in the same chat workspace never share one, and the same person on two services holds two.

Rules that always hold:

- The grant is kept with the moment it stops being valid, so it can be renewed quietly instead of being discovered dead mid-request.
- It outlives restarts and redeployments, because it is the one thing the user cannot re-supply without being asked again.
- Signing out removes it outright rather than letting it lapse.

The product's own registration with a service is separate: it is arranged once per service and shared by everyone, while the grant on top of it is always personal.

Lifecycle: none, then requested when a tool first needs it, then granted, then renewed for as long as the person keeps using it, and finally revoked on sign-out or abandoned when they never come back to finish.

nodes.name: Run Assistant
nodes.description:
Ask the assistant for an answer, with the tools it can reach and the exchanges it should remember.

- **Issued by**: the conversation round trip, always on one chat user's behalf.
- **Requires**: the user's message, whoever is speaking, any remembered exchanges, and an open connection to every configured tool provider.
- **Produces**: either one answer, or a set of sensitive actions held back for the user to confirm.
- **Fails as**: an answer in the wrong shape is retried up to three times; a sign-in the user was offered but never finished ends the run as an expected outcome rather than an error.

A resumed run, one that had held actions and is coming back with the user's decision, takes the same path with that decision already applied.

nodes.name: Open Tool Connections
nodes.description:
Reach every tool provider configured for this assistant, on behalf of the person the run is for, and hand the assistant the tools they expose.

- **Issued by**: the assistant run itself, before it asks the model anything.
- **Requires**: who the run is for. A provider expecting a sign-in also needs somewhere to keep it, otherwise the connection is refused outright rather than silently reaching the service as a stranger.
- **Produces**: one usable set of tools per provider, with every tool the provider marks destructive already flagged for confirmation.
- **Fails as**: a provider that expects a sign-in the user has not given pauses here while they are asked for one; a provider that cannot be reached at all fails the run.

The connections are per run and per person, never pooled, so one user's access is never handed to another.

nodes.name: Prepare Tool Access
nodes.description:
Open every tool connection without asking the assistant anything, purely so a sign-in the user still owes happens at a calm moment instead of interrupting their first real question.

- **Issued by**: the product, at a moment that is already about setup rather than about getting an answer. Today that is someone adding the assistant on LINE.
- **Requires**: who the person is.
- **Produces**: nothing the user sees directly, but it reports whether a sign-in actually took place, which decides whether they are greeted as newly connected or welcomed back.
- **Fails as**: an unfinished sign-in is an expected ending and the greeting is simply skipped; the user's next message picks the sign-in up again.

With no tool providers configured, it does nothing and reports that nothing happened.

nodes.name: Authorize Service
nodes.description:
Ask the user to grant the assistant access to one connected service, without making them leave the conversation.

- **Issued by**: the connection being opened, the moment it finds a service that expects a sign-in this person has not given.
- **Requires**: who the person is and which service is being reached.
- **Produces**: a sign-in link shown in the chat, and then a wait, four minutes by default, for the user to finish in their browser. What comes back is stored as their grant on that service.
- **Fails as**: the wait running out is an ordinary outcome, not an error. Their message goes unanswered and the next one offers the link again.

The wait is deliberately shorter than the connection's own patience, so a slow sign-in ends as an abandoned sign-in rather than as a broken service.

nodes.name: Complete Sign-In
nodes.description:
The user has finished granting access in their browser and lands back on the product's own return page; what they bring back is handed to the request still waiting for it.

- **Issued by**: the chat user, arriving from the connected service's own sign-in page.
- **Requires**: the one-time grant and the tag naming which waiting request it belongs to. A return missing either shows a failure page instead.
- **Produces**: the waiting request resumes and the user's access is stored; the page tells them, in their browser's language, that they can go back to the conversation.
- **Fails as**: a return that arrives after everyone has stopped waiting is simply discarded, and the user is asked again on their next message.

The tag travels back untouched so the service can check it against the one the sign-in started with, which is what stops somebody else's return from being substituted for theirs.

nodes.name: Revoke Authorization
nodes.description:
Sign the user out by removing their access to every connected service.

- **Issued by**: the assistant, when the user asks to sign out, log out, disconnect, or switch accounts. Because it is offered as a sensitive action, the user confirms it before it runs.
- **Requires**: who the person is. It exists at all only when sign-ins are configured; with none, the assistant is never offered it.
- **Produces**: every grant that person holds is gone, so their next request starts a fresh sign-in. It also marks the conversation's earlier exchanges as no longer true, because those answers assumed access that has just been taken away.
- **Fails as**: it does not. Repeating it on someone who holds nothing changes nothing.

Only the person's own grants are removed; the product's registration with each service is untouched and still serves everyone else.

driftIssues.description: The sign-out tool at src/conciergent/agent/runner.py:44-50 is named revoke_authorization and tells the user their authorization was removed, while the sign-out itself at src/conciergent/store/credential.py:74-78 only deletes the copy of the grant this product stored and sends no revocation to the connected service. The grant stays live at the service until it expires on its own, so a user who signs out to cut access off has not actually cut it off.

nodes.name: Sign-In Requested
nodes.description:
The user has been shown a link to grant the assistant access to one connected service.

Fires part-way through reaching that service, so the request that needed it is paused rather than finished, and the user has an answer waiting on them. What happens next is theirs: finish in the browser, or walk away and let the offer run out.

nodes.name: Service Authorized
nodes.description:
One person now has access to one connected service, kept along with the moment it stops being valid so it can be renewed later without asking them again.

Fires the moment their return from the browser reaches the request that was waiting, which then carries straight on to the tool it was trying to use. Everything they ask afterwards reuses this rather than asking again.

nodes.name: Sign-In Abandoned
nodes.description:
The user was shown the sign-in link and never came back in time.

This is an expected ending, not a failure: nothing is logged as broken and nothing is left half-granted. Their message goes unanswered, and the next one offers them the link again.

nodes.name: Authorization Revoked
nodes.description:
Every grant one person held on the connected services is gone, and their next request will start a fresh sign-in.

Fires while the turn is still running, before its answer reaches the user. It also crosses out of this subsystem: the conversation memory treats the earlier exchanges as no longer true, because they were built on access that no longer exists.

nodes.name: Destructive Actions Wait for the User's Yes
nodes.description:
A tool its provider marks as destructive never runs until the user has confirmed it. The marking comes from the provider, which is the only party that knows which of its own capabilities cannot be taken back, so it is trusted rather than second-guessed here. The product's own sign-out is held behind the same confirmation, because no provider marks it and it is every bit as hard to take back.

The business cares because the assistant acts on the user's real accounts with the user's own access. A single misread message would otherwise delete a document, cancel a booking, or empty a list, and none of that is something the user can undo by rephrasing. The cost of asking is one tap; the cost of not asking is unbounded.

The user sees a confirmation naming what is about to happen, with Confirm and Cancel. Applies to every tool of every provider and to the sign-out, on a first attempt and on a resumed one alike.

nodes.name: The Tools Are the Only Capability
nodes.description:
The assistant may only offer what its current tools can actually do. It never claims or invents a capability none of them expose.

The business cares because a confident promise the assistant cannot keep is worse than a plain refusal. The user acts on it, waits for something that never happens, and stops trusting the answers that were true. It matters most here because the tools differ per deployment, so the assistant genuinely cannot know its own reach without looking.

The user sees an honest "I cannot do that here" instead of a fabricated confirmation. Applies to every run.

nodes.name: Text From Tools Is Never an Instruction
nodes.description:
Anything that arrives in a tool result or an earlier exchange is information to work with, never a command to obey. Text sitting inside a name, a description, an email, or a file's contents is read as content even when it is phrased as an order.

The business cares because most of what the assistant reads was written by somebody other than the user, and the assistant is holding that user's own access to their real accounts. An instruction planted in a record the user merely asked about would otherwise spend that access on the planter's behalf, and the user would see only a plausible answer with something quietly done underneath it.

Nothing surfaces to the user when it holds. Applies to every run, to every provider's output and to the remembered conversation alike.

nodes.name: A Sign-In Belongs to One Person
nodes.description:
Access to a connected service is held against one person and one service together, and is never shared or reused for anybody else. The product's own registration with a service is arranged once and shared; the personal grant on top of it never is.

The business cares because sharing one would let a colleague in the same chat workspace act as somebody else on their real account, reading and changing things they were never entitled to touch, with the audit trail on the connected service naming the wrong person. Keeping the registration shared and the grant personal is what lets one deployment serve a whole team without pooling their access.

A violation would surface as the assistant answering with someone else's data. Applies to every read and every write of a stored sign-in.

nodes.name: A Sign-In Is Renewed, Not Re-Asked
nodes.description:
A stored grant is kept together with the moment it stops being valid, so it can be renewed before it is used rather than discovered dead when a tool is already running. It must also survive restarts and redeployments untouched.

The business cares because the alternative sends the user back through a sign-in they already completed, in the middle of asking for something else, on a schedule they cannot see and did nothing to cause. Access granted once should feel granted; being asked again reads as the product having forgotten them, and each extra sign-in is another chance to drop the request entirely.

The user sees nothing at all when it holds, which is the point. Applies to every stored sign-in on every service.

nodes.name: The Connection Waits Longer Than the User
nodes.description:
However long the user is given to complete a sign-in, the connection reaching that service must be willing to wait longer. The configuration refuses to start when it is set the other way round.

The business cares because the sign-in happens inside the attempt to reach the service. If the connection gives up first, an ordinary user taking a couple of minutes over a login page turns into a service that looks broken: the failure is logged as a real fault, the user gets nothing, and nobody can tell an outage from somebody who was simply reading carefully. With the order the right way round, the same slowness ends as an abandoned sign-in, which costs the user only their next message.

Applies to every deployment, checked once before the product will run at all.

nodes.name: One Confirmation Waits at a Time
nodes.description:
A conversation holds at most one waiting confirmation, and picking it up removes it. A newer confirmation takes the place of an older one, and once an answer has claimed a confirmation there is nothing left to claim again.

The business cares because a confirmation is answered by whatever the user says next, and there is only ever one next message. Two waiting at once would let a single Confirm settle the wrong held action, and a confirmation that survived being answered would let the same irreversible action run again on a later message.

Nothing surfaces to the user. A violation would show up as an action the user approved once happening twice, or a Confirm landing on something they never saw.

Applies to every waiting confirmation, for the whole life of a conversation.

nodes.name: An Unanswered Confirmation Ages Out
nodes.description:
A confirmation the user never answers stops waiting after a bounded time, ten minutes by default and adjustable per deployment. The held action is dropped with it, and the user's next message is answered as an ordinary fresh question.

The business cares because a held action only makes sense inside the conversation that raised it. Confirming it hours later would act on an intent the user has long since moved on from, and a confirmation held open forever would keep a stale irreversible action permanently one tap away.

Expiry is silent: the user sees no notice, just a normal answer to whatever they say next.

Applies to every waiting confirmation.

nodes.name: The Answer Is Matched Against the Words Offered
nodes.description:
A waiting confirmation carries its own Confirm and Cancel wording, and the user's answer is judged against that wording rather than against wording worked out afresh when they reply.

The business cares because the language a confirmation was written in cannot always be resolved a second time. On some chat platforms, tapping a button tells the product less about who is answering than sending a message does, so the reply would be read in a different language than the one the user was offered. The confirmation would then look like an unrelated remark, the action the user had just approved would be dropped in silence, and they would never be told it did not happen.

Applies whenever a waiting confirmation is answered, whether the user taps a button or types the words themselves.

nodes.name: A Return Is Matched to the Sign-In It Belongs To
nodes.description:
Every sign-in the assistant starts carries a one-time tag, and what the user brings back from the connected service is only accepted by the request holding that same tag. A link that arrives without a tag is refused before the user ever sees it, and a return missing either the grant or the tag is shown a short failure page instead.

The business cares because the return leg lands on an ordinary web address that anyone can call. Without the match, a grant obtained somewhere else could be handed to whichever request happened to be waiting, and one person's access to a connected service would end up stored against somebody else's name, with the service's own audit trail naming the wrong person.

The user sees nothing at all when it holds, and a short failure page when it does not. Applies to every sign-in, on every service and every chat platform.

nodes.name: The Sign-In Link Opens Outside the Chat App
nodes.description:
The link that starts a sign-in must open in the device's own browser rather than the small browser built into the chat app. On LINE the link is marked so the phone hands it to the real browser before the connected service is ever reached.

The business cares because connected services turn away a sign-in attempted from a chat app's built-in browser. Without this the user taps the button, is refused by the service with nothing they can do about it, and every tool behind that sign-in stays out of reach however many times they try.

The user notices only that the sign-in page opens the way any other link does. Applies wherever the chat platform opens links inside itself; platforms that already hand links to the browser need nothing extra.

nodes.name: An Unclaimed Return Is Thrown Away
nodes.description:
A grant that comes back from the connected service when nobody is waiting for it is held for five minutes and then discarded, instead of sitting in the store until something happens to pick it up.

The business cares because what comes back is a one-time key to somebody's real account. The request that asked for it may already have given up, or the process holding it may have restarted; leaving the key lying around is a standing risk for no gain, since a user who returns that late is asked to sign in again on their next message anyway.

The user sees nothing: a late return simply does nothing, and their next message offers the link afresh. Applies to every sign-in return on every service.

nodes.name: Reply Shape and Native Rendering
nodes.description:
An answer has to look at home wherever it lands. The same answer reaches one person in Slack, another in LINE, another in Discord, three products that draw a message three different ways and disagree about how long a title may be and which markup they will render at all. This subsystem owns the one shape an answer takes and how each chat platform paints it, so whoever writes the answer never has to know where it is going.

The terms this subsystem uses, and what each means here:

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| Reply | The single answer a turn produces: a short line, a card, or a set of option cards. |
| Card | A titled block with body paragraphs, an optional picture, link buttons, and follow-up buttons. |
| Option set | Up to four cards the user picks between, closed by an escape-hatch card. |
| Suggestion | A tappable follow-up; tapping it says its wording back to the assistant as if the user had typed it. |
| Rendering | One platform's own drawing of a reply, in that platform's message format. |
| Wording catalog | The product's own fixed copy, kept per key and per language apart from the code that shows it. |

Outside this boundary: deciding what the answer actually says, running the round trip that produces and dispatches it, receiving a button tap back off the platform, resolving which language a user reads in, and the credentials the chat apps post with. Those neighbours hand a finished answer in and get a sent message out; they never decide how it looks.

nodes.name: Structured Reply
nodes.description:
The one answer a turn produces, held in a form no chat platform owns: either a short line of text, a single card, or a small set of option cards.

A card carries a short title, up to six body paragraphs each optionally closing with a bulleted list, an optional picture above the title, a small footnote for caveats, up to five link buttons, and up to three follow-up suggestions. The first link is treated as the action the user is most likely to want and is drawn with emphasis. A suggestion is a shortcut rather than a decoration: it carries both the words on the button and the words said back to the assistant when it is tapped.

An option set is up to four of those cards for the user to pick between, always closed by an escape-hatch card for the case where none of them fit.

Why it is held apart from any platform: the answer is written once and drawn three ways. Sizes, wording, and structure are settled here, against the tightest platform, so the drawing step never has to negotiate with the content.

Lifecycle: created fresh at the end of every turn, handed once to the chat platform, never revised and never stored. Nothing else in the product refers back to a reply after it is sent.

nodes.name: Platform Rendering
nodes.description:
One chat platform's ability to draw an answer in its own message format, to signal that work is under way, and to tell the assistant what markup it will actually render.

Each platform contributes its own and keeps all of its own quirks inside it: LINE builds a scrollable bubble with its buttons either as chips beside the message or inside the bubble's footer, Slack builds a stack of blocks inside a color-striped attachment and threads it under the message being answered, Discord builds an embed with rows of buttons in the user's direct-message channel.

Why it exists: adding a chat platform should mean contributing one of these and nothing else, and changing how answers look should mean replacing one rather than changing what the assistant says. The colors it draws in are the ones whoever set the product up chose.

Lifecycle: built for one turn around the conversation being answered, used for that turn's sends, and discarded. It holds nothing between turns.

nodes.name: Interface Wording Catalog
nodes.description:
The product's own fixed copy, kept as keyed entries one per language, apart from the code that shows them. It covers everything the product says for itself rather than through the assistant: the sign-in card's title, body, and button, the confirm and cancel labels, the greetings, the status line on a tapped button, and the short browser pages shown after a sign-in or a workspace install completes.

Why it is a place of its own: this copy is the part a buyer wants to change. Keeping it keyed and separate makes rewording the product a matter of supplying a file, and adding a language a translation job rather than a code change.

Entries ship for English and Traditional Chinese. Whoever sets the product up can point it at their own folder and have their entries layered over the shipped ones, one key and one language at a time, leaving everything they did not mention on the shipped copy.

Lifecycle: assembled once when the product starts, replaced wholesale when custom wording is loaded, and read from memory on every lookup thereafter.

nodes.name: App Builder
nodes.description:
The person who sets this product up as their own assistant: they point it at their tools, connect their chat apps, and choose how it is worded and colored. They do not talk to it in a chat window, they configure it once and hand it to their users.

In this area their reach is the product's own copy and look: supplying their own wording for any key in any language, adding a language the product does not ship with, and choosing the brand and alert colors each platform's cards are drawn in. A person, not a system, and their choices apply to every user of that deployment rather than to one conversation.

nodes.name: Deliver the Reply
nodes.description:
Hand the finished answer to the chat platform, drawn the way that platform draws things.

- **Issued by**: the conversation round trip, once per turn, as soon as the assistant has answered.
- **Requires**: one finished answer and the rendering for the platform the conversation is on.
- **Produces**: exactly one message in the user's chat. A short line goes as plain text, a card as that platform's rich message, an option set as a group the user scrolls or picks through. A confirmation the user has to answer goes the same way, marked as sensitive so it is drawn as such.
- **Fails as**: this is the last step of the turn, so a platform that refuses the message loses the answer outright. There is no retry and no falling back to a plainer shape.

An option set is flattened on the way out: the escape-hatch card becomes the last card of the group, so the user meets it after the options rather than as a separate thing. Each platform's own ceiling still applies on top of the shared sizes, and Discord in particular drops any button past its fifth row, so a very button-heavy set can lose its tail.

nodes.name: Show That Work Is Under Way
nodes.description:
Tell the user their message has been picked up, before there is an answer to give them.

- **Issued by**: the conversation round trip, immediately after taking the message and before the assistant starts.
- **Requires**: nothing beyond the conversation being answered.
- **Produces**: whatever that platform offers. LINE runs its loading animation. Discord disables the buttons on a message the user just tapped, or shows a typing hint on an ordinary message. Slack rewrites the tapped message with its buttons disabled and a short line naming what is being processed, which the eventual answer then finalizes to a line naming what was selected.
- **Fails as**: quietly. The signal is reassurance, not part of the answer, so a failure is noted for operators and the turn carries on.

nodes.name: Ask What Markup the Platform Renders
nodes.description:
- **What the caller wants**: the writing rules for the platform this turn will land on. Whether it renders any markup at all, which flavor if it does, and how a link or a list should be written there.
- **Called by**: the assistant, once per turn, folded into its own instructions before it composes anything.
- **Freshness**: fixed per platform and always current. A platform that has nothing to say returns nothing and the assistant writes as it would anywhere.

nodes.name: Look Up Interface Wording
nodes.description:
- **What the caller wants**: one line of the product's own copy, in the user's language, with any values filled in, such as the workspace being installed into or the action awaiting confirmation.
- **Called by**: everything that shows fixed copy. The sign-in card, the confirmation card, the greeting after a sign-in completes, the status line on a tapped button, and the short browser pages the user lands on coming back from a service.
- **Freshness**: read straight from memory, always reflecting whatever custom wording was loaded at startup.

A key with no entry in the user's language is answered in English rather than left blank.

nodes.name: Load Custom Wording
nodes.description:
Layer someone's own copy over the wording the product ships with.

- **Issued by**: whoever set the product up, by pointing its configuration at a folder of wording files.
- **Requires**: one or more folders holding a file per language, each file naming its language.
- **Produces**: a catalog carrying their entries on top of the shipped ones, key by key and language by language, with everything they did not mention left on the shipped copy. Later folders win over earlier ones. Every part of the product that shows copy picks the change up without being told.
- **Fails as**: a file whose name is not a language the product knows is passed over rather than treated as a mistake, so an unrelated file sitting in the folder does not stop startup.

nodes.name: An Answer Is Sized for the Tightest Platform
nodes.description:
Every part of an answer carries a hard size limit chosen so the same answer renders everywhere: a title of at most 40 characters, at most six body paragraphs of 100 characters each, at most ten items in one bulleted list, at most five link buttons and three follow-up suggestions, and at most four cards in an option set. A suggestion's visible label stops at 20 characters and the words it says back at 40.

The business cares because the limits are not the same on every platform and the tightest one wins. An answer written for the roomiest platform arrives on another cut off mid-sentence, or is refused outright, and the user gets nothing back for a message they took the trouble to send.

An oversized answer is turned away before it can be sent and the assistant is asked again, up to three times. Applies to every card and every option set, whatever the platform, including the cards the product writes for itself.

nodes.name: Card Wording Is Plain, the Platform Adds the Styling
nodes.description:
Text inside a card is written as plain wording with no markup: no bold, no addresses written inline, and no bullet characters typed into list items. The bullet marker, the emphasis, and the button all come from the platform's own drawing.

The business cares because a card is not free text, it is assembled from named parts. Markup typed into a part shows up literally as stray asterisks and brackets in the middle of a sentence on a platform that does not parse it, and doubles up with the marker the drawing already adds. A bullet character that slips in anyway is stripped before drawing rather than shown twice.

The user never sees the rule holding; they see it failing as a title reading like source code. Applies to every card, including the sign-in and confirmation cards the product writes itself.

nodes.name: A Plain Answer Is Written in the Platform's Own Markup
nodes.description:
When the answer is a short line rather than a card, it is written in the markup the receiving platform actually renders, and the assistant is told which that is before it writes a word.

The three differ enough to matter. LINE renders none, so a list is written with a bullet character and ideas are separated by blank lines. Slack renders its own flavor, where bold takes a single asterisk and a link is written as the address and its words together. Discord renders ordinary markdown but shows links as bare addresses, so the address is written plainly rather than hidden behind words.

The business cares because the same line reads as a clean answer on one platform and as a mess of stray asterisks and brackets on another. The user has no way to know it was written for somewhere else; it simply looks broken.

Applies to the plain-text shape only. Cards carry no markup at all.

nodes.name: Every Option Can Be Picked
nodes.description:
Each card in an option set carries the means of choosing it, either a follow-up suggestion or a link, and the set always closes with an escape-hatch card for the case where none of the options fit.

The business cares because an option set is a question put to the user. An option they can read but not act on is worse than not having offered it, and a set with no way out corners someone whose answer is not on the list into retyping their request from scratch.

The user meets the escape hatch as the last card after the options. Applies to option sets only; a single card carries no such requirement.

nodes.name: Missing Wording Falls Back to English
nodes.description:
When the product's own copy has no entry for the user's language, the English entry is shown rather than failing or leaving a gap.

The business cares because this copy grows a language at a time and custom wording is written by hand. A missing entry would otherwise break the very thing it labels, a sign-in card with no button words or a confirmation with nothing to confirm, and strand the user at exactly the moment they need to act. English is a worse experience than their own language and a far better one than nothing.

The user sees one line in English inside an otherwise translated message. Applies to every piece of the product's own copy, shipped or supplied, and not to what the assistant writes, which is composed in the user's language each turn.

nodes.name: Interface Wording Lives in the Catalog
nodes.description:
Every fixed line the product says for itself, button labels, card titles, greetings, and the browser pages a user lands on, is held in the wording catalog under a key. It is never written into the code that shows it and never into the configuration file next to credentials and colors.

The business cares because this copy is precisely the part a buyer wants to make their own: their tone, their brand, their language. Holding it in one keyed place is what turns rewording the whole product into supplying a file, and adding a language into a translation job rather than a code change. Copy scattered across the code cannot be handed to a translator at all.

Applies to everything the product says on its own behalf. It does not apply to what the assistant says, which is written fresh each turn.

nodes.name: A Progress Signal Never Costs the Answer
nodes.description:
The hint that work is under way, the loading animation, the typing indicator, the tapped button turning into a status line, is cosmetic. When it cannot be shown, the failure is noted quietly for operators and the turn carries straight on to produce the answer.

The business cares because the signal exists to reassure someone during a wait. Letting it end the turn would trade the entire answer for the reassurance that one was coming, which is the worst exchange available.

The user sees a wait with no indicator and then their answer as usual. Applies to every progress signal on every platform, including the one that rewrites a message the user just tapped.

nodes.name: A Confirmation Reads as Dangerous
nodes.description:
A card asking the user to confirm something that may not be undone is drawn apart from an ordinary answer: in the alert color rather than the brand color, with the confirming button emphasized over the others, and with the whole set of buttons marked as spent by the first tap so the question is not answered twice.

The business cares because that tap is the last thing standing between the user and something irreversible. A confirmation that looks like every other card gets tapped the way every other card gets tapped, and the safeguard becomes a formality the user clicks through.

The user sees a visibly different card and a button that stops responding once they have answered. Applies wherever a held action is put to the user, on every platform, and to nothing else.

nodes.name: Message Arrival and User Identity
nodes.description:
A person types into Slack, LINE, or Discord, and what reaches this product is a signed web request or a frame on an open socket, not yet a question worth answering. Something has to prove the delivery really came from the platform it claims, drop what is not a person talking, refuse to act on the same delivery twice, and work out which person is speaking and in which conversation. This subsystem owns that doorway, and the identity everything downstream is attributed to.

The terms this subsystem uses, and what each means here:

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| Delivery | One thing a chat platform handed over: a typed message, a tap on a suggestion, or somebody adding the assistant. |
| Identity | The stable handle naming one person: the platform, the workspace or account, and their account within it. |
| Conversation | The scope memory and waiting confirmations belong to, decided here from the identity plus the thread the delivery arrived in. |
| Installation | The product's presence in one Slack workspace, and the credential it answers that workspace with. |
| Connection | A link held open to a platform that pushes its deliveries rather than posting them. |

Three platforms arrive two different ways: Slack and LINE post signed requests, Discord streams over a connection this product keeps open. Both paths end the same way, in one accepted message attributed to one person.

Outside this boundary: what a turn actually does with the message, how the answer is drawn for each platform, and the personal sign-ins the assistant's tools need. Those neighbours receive an accepted message and an identity; they never decide whether a delivery was genuine or whose it was.

nodes.name: Inbound Delivery
nodes.description:
One thing a chat platform handed over, and whether it earns an answer. A delivery is only a candidate: most of what platforms send is not a person asking something, and the same delivery often arrives more than once because the platform retried it.

Rules that always hold:

- A delivery that cannot prove it came from the platform is refused outright.
- Only a person's own direct message or their tap on a suggestion starts a turn; anything from a bot, an edit, or a group channel is dropped.
- The same delivery is acted on once, however many times the platform sends it.
- The platform is told the delivery landed before the answer is produced, because platforms give only seconds.

Lifecycle:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Arrived
    Arrived --> Refused: signature does not check out
    Arrived --> Ignored: not a person talking, or already seen
    Arrived --> Accepted: genuine, eligible, first time
    Accepted --> [*]: handed to a turn
```

A delivery reaches the person it belongs to and the workspace credential needed to answer through their identities, never by carrying either itself.

nodes.name: Platform Connection
nodes.description:
The link this product holds open to a platform that pushes its deliveries instead of posting them, today Discord. While the link is up, messages and taps arrive on it; while it is down, that platform's users get nothing, so keeping it up is the whole job.

Rules that always hold:

- A connection the platform rejected outright is not retried, because the same rejection would repeat forever.
- A connection that merely dropped is re-established, waiting longer between attempts, and picks up the stream where it left off rather than replaying it.

Each platform runs on its own, so one platform's link failing leaves the others answering normally.

nodes.name: User Identity
nodes.description:
Who is speaking, and everything the product keeps about them between messages: the stable handle that names them, the conversation their message belongs to, and the language they read in.

The handle is built from the platform, the workspace or account, and the person's account within it, so the same human in two Slack workspaces counts as two people and shares neither memory nor sign-ins. It is derived fresh from every delivery rather than stored, which is what makes it stable.

The one thing that is kept is the language, remembered per person so a later message can be answered in it even when that message carries no clue about which language they read.

Everything a turn does is attributed to this identity: the memory it reads, the confirmations it holds, and the personal sign-ins it uses.

nodes.name: Workspace Installation
nodes.description:
The product's presence inside one Slack workspace: the credential it posts with there, and a record of who put it there.

One deployment can serve many workspaces at once, each answered with its own credential, so a workspace that removes the app stops being answerable without affecting the rest. A single-workspace deployment can skip the whole flow and configure one credential up front, which answers any workspace no stored credential is found for.

Adding a workspace is a browser round trip away from the chat app: the product sends the person to Slack, Slack sends them back, and only a return that matches the request that started it is honoured.

nodes.name: Accept an Arriving Message
nodes.description:
Decide whether something a platform just delivered is a genuine, first-time message from a person, and if it is, hand it on to be answered.

- **Issued by**: the chat user, relayed by whichever platform received their message or their tap.
- **Requires**: proof the delivery came from the platform, and content that is a person talking rather than a bot echo, an edit, or a group message.
- **Produces**: an accepted message, attributed to one person and one conversation, or nothing at all.
- **Fails as**: a delivery that cannot prove its origin is refused with an authentication error; everything else that does not qualify is dropped silently, because a platform reads a complaint as a reason to retry.

nodes.name: Hold the Platform Connection
nodes.description:
Keep the link to a pushing platform open for as long as the product runs, so that platform's messages have somewhere to arrive.

- **Issued by**: the product itself at start-up, once per platform that pushes.
- **Requires**: a working credential for that platform.
- **Produces**: a live link that delivers messages and taps until the product stops.
- **Fails as**: a rejected credential ends that platform's link for good and is reported; a dropped link is simply re-established.

nodes.name: Work Out Who Is Speaking
nodes.description:
Turn what a platform said about a delivery into the handle that names the person and the conversation their message belongs to.

- **Issued by**: the doorway, on every delivery it accepts.
- **Requires**: the platform, the workspace or account the delivery came through, and the person's account there.
- **Produces**: a stable handle for the person, and the conversation scope their memory and any waiting confirmation live under.
- **Fails as**: an account whose name would make the handle ambiguous is rejected rather than quietly reshaped.

nodes.name: Remember the User's Language
nodes.description:
Record the language a person reads in, learned from whatever the platform said about them, so later messages can be answered in it.

- **Issued by**: the doorway, whenever a delivery carries a language and the platform does not offer one on demand.
- **Requires**: the person's handle and the language the delivery carried.
- **Produces**: a remembered language for that person, replacing whatever was remembered before.
- **Fails as**: a language the product does not recognise is discarded rather than stored, and the reply falls back.

driftIssues.description: Slack and LINE read the user's language from the platform profile on every delivery (src/conciergent/surfaces/slack/surface.py:50-65, src/conciergent/surfaces/line/surface.py:56-67); Discord has no profile lookup and only learns the language when the user taps a button, at src/conciergent/surfaces/discord/gateway.py:258-267. A Discord user who only ever types is answered in the fallback language indefinitely.

nodes.name: Install Into a Workspace
nodes.description:
Put the assistant into a Slack workspace and keep the credential it will answer there with.

- **Issued by**: the person setting the product up for their team.
- **Requires**: a return from Slack that matches the request that started it, and a code Slack has not already spent.
- **Produces**: a stored credential for that workspace, tagged with who installed it, and a page telling the installer it worked.
- **Fails as**: a declined install, a mismatched return, or a spent code all end on the same failure page; none of them is treated as a fault of the product.

nodes.name: Greet Someone Who Just Added the Assistant
nodes.description:
Welcome a person the moment they add the assistant, and use that moment to get any sign-in they will need out of the way before they ask their first question.

- **Issued by**: the platform, when somebody adds the assistant; supported on LINE today.
- **Requires**: the new person's handle.
- **Produces**: either a welcome saying the assistant is ready, or one saying it is ready again, depending on whether a sign-in was completed just now.
- **Fails as**: a person handed a sign-in link who walks away gets no greeting; the welcome waits for their first message instead.

driftIssues.description: LINE reacts when somebody adds the assistant and greets them, getting any sign-in out of the way up front, at src/conciergent/surfaces/line/webhook.py:99-109; the Slack delivery route at src/conciergent/surfaces/slack/webhook.py:212 acts only on a message and the Discord connection at src/conciergent/surfaces/discord/gateway.py:164-169 acts only on ready, message and button events, so neither notices the assistant being added. A Slack or Discord user gets no welcome and meets the sign-in request in the middle of their first real question instead of before it.

nodes.name: Look Up the User's Language
nodes.description:
Find the language to answer a person in.

Asked once per delivery, before anything is written, so the reply, the confirmation card, and any sign-in prompt all read the same way. Answered from the platform's own profile where the platform offers one, and from what was remembered about the person otherwise. An unknown answer is fine: the product falls back rather than guessing.

nodes.name: Message Accepted
nodes.description: A genuine, first-time message from an identified person is ready to be answered. Fires at the end of the doorway, once the delivery has proved its origin, qualified as a person talking, and been checked as one the product has not already acted on. The turn lifecycle reacts by running the round trip; nothing inside the doorway does.

nodes.name: Assistant Added
nodes.description: Somebody has just added the assistant on their platform. Fires when the platform reports the addition rather than a message, and is answered with a welcome instead of a turn. Stays inside the doorway.

nodes.name: Workspace Installed
nodes.description: A Slack workspace now has the assistant, and the credential to answer there has been stored. Fires at the end of the browser round trip, after the return has been matched to the request that started it. Nothing reacts automatically; from here on, messages from that workspace are answerable.

nodes.name: A Delivery Must Prove Where It Came From
nodes.description:
Every delivery carries a signature made with a secret only the product and the platform share, and a delivery whose signature does not check out is refused before anything is read from it. Slack deliveries must also be recent: one whose timestamp is more than five minutes off is refused as stale.

The business cares because the address a platform posts to is public. Without the check, anybody who found it could impersonate a user, make the assistant answer questions nobody asked, and spend the account's usage doing it, while the conversation history filled with exchanges the real person never had.

A refused delivery is answered with an authentication error and nothing else happens. Applies to every delivery on every platform that posts.

driftIssues.description: Slack refuses a delivery whose timestamp is more than five minutes off at src/conciergent/surfaces/slack/webhook.py:196-206; the LINE check at src/conciergent/surfaces/line/webhook.py:166-170 verifies only the signature and has no freshness window. A captured LINE delivery stays replayable indefinitely, and only the event-id check stops it being answered again.

nodes.name: Only a Person's Direct Message Starts a Turn
nodes.description:
A turn starts only for a person's own message in a direct conversation with the assistant, or their tap on a suggestion the assistant offered. Messages from bots, edits and other after-the-fact changes, empty messages, and anything in a shared or group channel are dropped without a reply.

The business cares because the assistant lives in the same chat apps as everything else a team says. Answering group chatter would make it interrupt conversations it was never part of, and answering another bot would let two automated participants talk to each other indefinitely, at a real cost per exchange.

Nothing is surfaced when a delivery is dropped; the platform is simply told it landed. Applies at the doorway, before any identity or memory is touched.

nodes.name: The Same Delivery Is Acted On Once
nodes.description:
A delivery is recorded the first time it is acted on and ignored on every later arrival, for a day afterwards. A tap that closes a set of options counts for the whole set, so a person cannot pick twice from one card; a tap that leaves the options standing counts per button, so different follow-ups from the same card each get their turn.

The business cares because platforms retry a delivery they think went unanswered, and a duplicate turn means the same question answered twice, the same action taken twice, and the same confirmation raised twice for something the user already approved.

A repeat is dropped silently. Applies to every delivery the doorway accepts.

driftIssues.description: Slack and Discord deduplicate every delivery they act on (src/conciergent/surfaces/slack/webhook.py:77 and src/conciergent/surfaces/discord/gateway.py:181); LINE skips the check when the delivery carries no event id, at src/conciergent/surfaces/line/webhook.py:64-68. A LINE delivery without an id that the platform retries is answered twice.

nodes.name: The Platform Is Answered Before the User Is
nodes.description:
The platform is told its delivery landed straight away, and the answer is produced afterwards, out of band. Platforms allow only a few seconds before treating a delivery as failed.

The business cares because an answer worth waiting for almost always takes longer than the platform will wait: the assistant may think, call a tool, or pause for a confirmation. Holding the platform open until the answer is ready would make every real question look like a failure and be retried, so the user would get their answer two or three times over.

A violation shows up as duplicate answers rather than as an error. Applies to every accepted delivery.

driftIssues.description: Slack and LINE acknowledge the platform first and produce the answer on a background task (src/conciergent/surfaces/slack/webhook.py:79-92, src/conciergent/surfaces/line/webhook.py:69-77); the Discord connection produces the answer inline in the loop that reads the stream, at src/conciergent/surfaces/discord/gateway.py:172-185. While one Discord answer is being produced, that platform's later deliveries wait behind it.

nodes.name: A Person Is Named by Platform, Workspace, and Account
nodes.description:
A person's handle is built from three parts joined in a fixed order: the platform they are on, the workspace or account the message came through, and their account within it. None of the parts may contain the separator, so a handle can always be read back into the parts it was built from.

The business cares because this handle is what memory, waiting confirmations, and personal sign-ins are filed under. Two people whose handles collided would read each other's conversation and act with each other's access; a handle that could not be read back would strand whatever was filed under it.

A part that would make the handle ambiguous is rejected outright rather than quietly reshaped. Applies everywhere a person is named, on every platform.

nodes.name: The User's Language Is Learned From What Arrives
nodes.description:
Where a platform will tell the product what language a person reads, it is asked once per delivery and the answer is used for everything written in that turn. Where a platform mentions the language on only some deliveries, it is remembered the first time it appears and reused afterwards.

The business cares because a person should not have to state their language, and should not get an English reply to a question they asked in their own. Asking once per turn also keeps one reply from mixing languages between its text, its buttons, and any sign-in prompt.

Until a language is known the product falls back rather than guessing. Applies to every person on every platform.

nodes.name: Each Workspace Is Answered With Its Own Credential
nodes.description:
A message from a workspace is answered with the credential stored for that workspace. A deployment serving a single workspace may configure one credential up front, which is used for any workspace no stored credential is found for.

The business cares because one deployment is meant to serve many teams. Answering one workspace with another's credential would post the reply into the wrong company's chat, and a workspace that removed the app must simply stop being answerable rather than fall back onto somebody else's access.

When no credential can be found the message goes unanswered and nothing is recorded. Applies to every reply and every prompt sent back to a workspace.

nodes.name: An Install Return Is Matched to the Request That Started It
nodes.description:
Sending somebody to Slack to install the assistant stashes a one-shot token that the return must present. The token is consumed on first use and expires ten minutes after it was issued, so a return presenting an unknown, reused, or stale token is refused.

The business cares because without the match, a link crafted by somebody else could make an admin install an attacker's app under the team's name, or replay an old install to overwrite the workspace's credential.

A refused return shows the installer the same failure page as any other unsuccessful install. Applies to every workspace install.

nodes.name: A Rejected Connection Is Not Retried
nodes.description:
When a platform closes the connection with a reason saying the product itself is not acceptable, a bad credential or permissions it was never granted, that platform is given up on rather than retried.

The business cares because the rejection would repeat identically on every attempt: an endless reconnect loop hides a misconfiguration only a person can fix, and can get the product rate-limited or blocked by the platform. Failing loudly and once is what gets it noticed and corrected.

The failure is reported and only that platform stops; the others keep answering. Applies to every platform the product holds a connection to.

nodes.name: A Dropped Connection Picks Up Where It Left Off
nodes.description:
A connection that drops for any ordinary reason is re-established, waiting a little longer before each further attempt up to a minute, and asks the platform to continue the stream from the last delivery it saw rather than starting clean.

The business cares because dropped links are routine and users notice only the gap. Resuming means messages sent during the gap still arrive, so a question asked at the wrong moment is answered late instead of never, and backing off keeps a platform outage from turning into a flood of reconnects.

A link whose heartbeat goes unanswered is treated as dropped even when it still looks open. Applies to every platform the product holds a connection to.

nodes.name: Setup and Startup
nodes.description:
Getting the product running should not require writing code. Someone who wants their own tools to have a chat face writes one settings file, points it at their tool servers and their chat platforms, and starts it. That whole path is what this subsystem owns, from the starter file it hands them to the moment the product is live and listening.

The words used here:

- **Configuration** — the one file the person setting the product up writes. Everything the product can be told is in it, and anything left out falls back to a shipped value.
- **Platform** — Slack, LINE or Discord. Each has its own switch and only runs when switched on.
